synopsis: Open-source tools are viable as a low-license-cost simulation core, but do not provide the lowest total cost; even free software can underpin a program costing seven figures annually because of engineering labor [f196, f8296, f13551]. Public tool prices are almost entirely absent and nearly every commercial tool is quote-only, so budgets should use vendor quotations; the few dated price points found include an unofficial January 2024 MathWorks list, a Falcon education license, an NI controller and cloud GPU rates [f8304, f8305, f16441]. License permissions vary by component and use: Isaac Sim's core is Apache 2.0 and free for internal R&D, but some assets have additional terms and redistribution with Omniverse Kit requires NVIDIA AI Enterprise, whose price was not found [f8483, f8484, f8486]. Procurement should price peak concurrent workers, continuous-integration and cloud rights, subcontractor access, HIL nodes and disaster recovery rather than desktop seats alone; marketplace asset terms may also prohibit redistribution or training use [f16486, f4373]. The plan needs ownership, budget, licences and revalidation rules after September 2027, an identified sustainment blind spot; supplier rights still under negotiation near prototype delivery and unbudgeted license invoices are warning signs [f10179, f10367, f11025, f11083].
